#### PREFACE TO THE PAPERBACK EDITION

If you are reading this book in China, you might have a drone hovering outside your window. What’s it doing there?

The world has been rocked by the COVID-19 pandemic. In such moments of existential crisis and visceral fear, most people turn to a powerful government for security and safety. After all, we do need coordination, leadership, and public services to see us through this episode. This is exactly how the philosopher Thomas Hobbes saw things in the 1640s, as the English Civil War was raging, when he argued that people should "submit their Wills" to an all-powerful state, a Leviathan, which would then provide security and prosperity.

It hasn’t always been like this. Most of our existence on this planet, for about 200,000 years, has been in the context of what anthropologists call "small-scale societies," which did not have state-like institutions. It would not have occurred to those ancestors of ours to submit their will to anybody, let alone to a state, in their hour of need. When states finally appeared on the scene, they weren’t the types of states that would bring security and safety, and certainly not against pandemics. Even the best among them, such as the Roman state, provided merely bread and circuses, and only if you happened to live in the capital, Rome. Their citizens would not have trusted the state much either. So how did we end up in a world where we depend on governments and expect much more from them than our ancestors could imagine?

In China, whose state institutions Thomas Hobbes would have approved of, citizens are presumed to have submitted their will to their rulers, and it has become accepted that the state can and should do more. Indeed, the drones are there to do more—to impose a lockdown and make sure that people don’t leave home, so that social distancing can be maintained. Then there is the app you need on your phone: If it gives you a green screen, you are healthy and good to move about. But what if you get red? And just how did it decide you were red? Did it take your temperature? Can other things give you a red too? Is monitoring social distancing the only thing the drone is doing?

Even if you don’t like the drones above you, the Chinese response seems preferable to what’s going on in many other parts of the world. Nothing much is happening in sub-Saharan Africa. That shouldn’t be surprising. Most countries in the continent don’t have functioning state institutions. In the terminology we introduce in Chapter 11, they have "Paper Leviathans" that pretend to be all-powerful but are in truth paper-thin.

More shocking is what’s going on in the United States. The government, led by President Trump, went from denial to bumbling. Trump attempted to get the private sector involved in building essential medical equipment, until he got exasperated; on March 27 he angrily tweeted: "As usual with ‘this’ General Motors, things just never seem to work out. They said they were going to give us 40,000 much needed Ventilators, ‘very quickly’. Now they are saying it will only be 6000, in late April, and they want top dollar . . . Invoke ‘P’." P is the Cold War–era Defense Production Act, which gives the president the authority to order companies to make things. Sort of a China-lite strategy. Is that where the United States should be heading? Is there a different path? Could we have government leadership and coordination for a powerful response to the pandemic without succumbing to the drones?

These are the questions we address in this book. We didn’t write it with the COVID-19 pandemic in mind. But if we had invented a scenario to illustrate the book’s main ideas, we could never have come up with one so fitting. This is because the answers to those questions all revolve around the central thesis of our book: It is the way the state and society interact and control each other that determines the capacity of our state, the policies of our government, and our resilience, prosperity, security, and ultimately, liberty.

The book explains why we should indeed expect countries around the world to respond so differently to the pandemic, and it clarifies the costs as well as the benefits of the Chinese strategy of draconian control over society (named after an Athenian ruler, Draco, whom you’ll meet in Chapter 2).

To start with, not everything that governments do is deal with pandemics. The Chinese strategy, a perfect specimen of the response from what we call a "Despotic Leviathan," works less well when it comes to other things, such as delivering justice, encouraging innovation and experimentation, and protecting liberty. The unchecked power of the state that can control people’s behavior in order to halt the spread of a virus can also control them when they dissent, can imprison them, repress them, and even murder them, as the Chinese state is currently doing in parts of the country, particularly in Xinjiang.

It is not even clear that despotism works best against pandemics. True, the U.S. government ignored the danger, vacillated, and bungled its response, but China first covered up the pandemic and is now controlling and even limiting scientific research and dissemination of vital information on the virus. In one day, the number of fatalities from COVID-19 in Wuhan was retrospectively increased by 50 percent. Do we really know the right number? Probably not, because China actively censors information. But do the Chinese authorities know the right number? That’s also unclear, since people may not provide the correct information when they mistrust the state and fear it. Are drones and apps substitutes for trust and cooperation and legitimacy in the eyes of citizens? How effective can a state really be when it locks up its people arbitrarily and censors them?

The more fundamental question is this: Do we have a choice other than between the despotism of the Chinese state and the dysfunction of sub-Saharan Africa or, in a milder form, the chaotic response of the Trump administration? Do we have to settle for one of those two evils? This is the fundamental question posed by Friedrich von Hayek, whom we’ll encounter in Chapter 15, during a critical episode of the twentieth century, the reconstruction of state and society after the Great Depression of 1929 and World War II. Hayek worried that if we gave too much power to and demanded too much from the state, it would inevitably be like the Chinese Leviathan. We’ll explain why Hayek’s concerns were valid (after all, dominance over society is in the DNA of the state, and it is hard to take powers back once you give them to the Leviathan). Nonetheless, Hayek’s pessimism was misplaced. This is because, squeezed between the absence of functional state institutions and the despotism of their dominance over society, there is a narrow corridor where society actively balances the state, monitors its powers, disagrees with it and contests it when necessary, and sometimes even cooperates with it. It is in this corridor that the deepest form of state capacity develops (because it is here that society can trust the state and share information and responsibility with it), and it is also in this corridor that society’s active participation in politics can grow together with the state’s power and capacity. Indeed, this is what happened in most of the West after World War II and why Hayek’s fears of unadulterated state despotism did not come to pass. But we’ll also explain why the corridor is narrow and why life in it is treacherous and requires hard work from citizens, who need to remain vigilant, organized, and politically active.

Will the pandemic change the world in ways we could not have imagined six months ago? Probably (though major changes may have been due even without the pandemic; think soaring inequality, enduring poverty, discontent against globalization and immigration, and the rise of populism and nationalism). But our future is not preordained, nor does it consist of an unsavory choice between a crumbling public health care infrastructure and drones monitoring our every move. What these different futures are and how we can influence ours are among the questions this book addresses.

Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson

April 2020

### 3. Books by One or by Multiple Authors

The basic format for a footnote referencing a book by one author is:

1. First name Last name, Title of Book (City: Publisher, date), #.

The basic format for a bibliographical entry for a book is:

Last name, First name. Title of Book. City: Publisher, date.

Book by one author – examples footnote format

1. Ann Burlein, Lift High the Cross: Where White Supremacy and the Christian Right Converge (Durham: Duke University Press, 2002), 14.

2. Sean McCloud, Making the American Religious Fringe: Exotics, Subversives, and Journalists, 1955-1993 (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina University Press, 2004), 163.

Book by one author – examples of bibliographical format

Burlein, Ann. Lift High the Cross: Where White Supremacy and the Christian Right Converge. Durham: Duke University Press, 2002.

McCloud, Sean. Making the American Religious Fringe: Exotics, Subversives, and Journalists, 1955-1993. Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina University Press, 2004.

### 4. Chapters and Essays in Edited Books

The basic format for a footnote referencing an article or chapter in an edited book is:

1. First name Last name, “Title of Article,” in Title of Book, ed. First name Last Name (City: Publisher, date), #.

The basic separator in a footnote is a comma, and the first word after a comma is not capitalized unless it is a proper name.

The basic format for a bibliographical entry for an article or chapter in an edited book is:

Last name, First name. “Title of the Article.” In Title of Book, ed. First name Last name, ##-##. City: Publisher, date.

The basic separator in a bibliographical entry is a period, and the first word after a period is capitalized just like the first word in a next sentence after a period. Note that the inclusive page numbers of the entire article or chapter are included in the bibliographical entry.

Edited books – examples of footnote format

1. Kathryn Johnson, “The Lessons of the Garden: An Examination of the Scriptural Legacy of Islam,” in Living Traditions of the Bible, ed. James E. Bowley (St. Louis: Chalice Press, 1999), 108.

2. Reuven Firestone, “The Qur’ān and the Bible: Some Modern Studies of Their Relationship,” in Bible and Qur’an: Essays in Scriptural Intertextuality, ed. John C. Reeves (Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 2003), 11.

Edited books – examples of bibliographical format

Johnson, Kathryn. “The Lessons of the Garden: An Examination of the Scriptural Legacy of Islam.” In Living Traditions of the Bible, edited by James E. Bowley, 103-31. St. Louis: Chalice Press,1999.

Firestone, Reuven. “The Qur’ān and the Bible: Some Modern Studies of Their Relationship.” in Bible and Qur’ān: Essays in Scriptural Intertextuality, edited by John C. Reeves, 1-22. Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 2003.

Note: If you are citing text written by the editor of the book, the footnote references the editor, and the listing in the bibliography is placed under the editor’s name.

If you are citing an article written by a contributor other than the editor, the footnote references the author of the article, and the book is listed in the bibliography under the contributor’s name rather than the editor’s name.

### 5. Articles in Journals

The basic format referencing an article in a journal is:

1. First name Last name, “Title of Article,” Name of Journal volume # (year) : #.

The basic format for a bibliographical entry for an article in a journal is:

Last name, First name. “Title of Article.” Name of Journal. volume # (year) : ##-##.

Note that the inclusive page numbers of the entire article are included in the bibliographical entry.

Journal Article – Examples of footnote format

1. John C. Reeves, “Exploring the Afterlife of Jewish Pseudepigrapha in Medieval Near Eastern Religious Traditions: Some Initial Soundings,” Journal for the Study of Judaism 30 (1999) : 150.

2. James D. Tabor, “Why 2K? The Biblical Roots of Millennialism,” Bible Review 15.6 (1999) : 26.

Journal Article – Examples of bibliographical format

Reeves, John C. “Exploring the Afterlife of Jewish Pseudepigrapha in Medieval Near Eastern Religious Traditions: Some Initial Soundings.” Journal for the Study of Judaism 30 (1999) : 148-177.

Tabor, James D. “Why 2K? The Biblical Roots of Millennialism.” Bible Review 15.6 (1999) : 16-27, 44-45.

Making the Difficult Marriage Work In their book The Narrow Corridor, Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson offer a complementary perspective on the fragile balances that allow a free society to work.[41] The challenge, they argue, is created by the need for a state—the “Leviathan” in the terminology of the seventeenth-century political philosopher Thomas Hobbes—strong enough to provide security and protection to the people, but not so strong as to deprive them of their freedoms. There is, then, a narrow corridor between the two extremes where the interaction between the state and civil society works. It is where a “shackled,” but strong, Leviathan and an engaged civil society exist side by side.[42] In other words, it is the liberal democracy discussed above. In fact, the general notion that the tales are not what they seem may be what most fully unifies scholars at odds with one another; a sort of harmony, then, exists because each interpreter acknowledges that there is pleasure in seeing how many differences can arise from the same source (259). This unifying aporia depends on difference: opposites are symbiotic. Nodelman’s technique in his willingness to concede does not make him a fence-straddler; on the contrary, such an outlook prioritizes pleasure over the potentially misleading academic task of resolving inconsistencies. Embracing the unclear for the sake of pleasure puts symbolic significance in its place while also not rejecting it as unimportant; the orange contains such paradox. The orange in literature stands on a boundary between two states of being: it separates the everyday world from a place more wondrous, more exotic, but out of reach. One might ask whether the emblem spanning two sides unites more or divides more. Because one major literary convention in the context of Christianity—fruit preceding a fall—gets depicted most often with apples instead of oranges, one might argue that there is, so to speak, no comparison between the two. In both prelapsarian and postlapsarian reference (which, seen in the right context, effectively covers all of time), the apple would seem to be the bigger star. However, the orange in literature for and about children holds a distinct edge over other fruit as symbol. Because of the orange’s aporetic connection of promising escape while simultaneously calling attention to one’s entrapment or while signifying deep values not immediately attainable, oranges, in at least this frame, may indeed be the only fruit. According to John McPhee in what certainly must be the definitive book on oranges, simply entitled Oranges, these are the only fruits which are sweeter when grown closer to the equator and which require northern latitudes for their distinctive tartness (4).
